Yes—these papers describe automated fact-checking/verification systems that decide whether an image-based input is reliable and help assess whether an image supports (or conflicts with) an associated claim. For example, VILLAIN verifies image-text claims using vision-language agents that retrieve evidence, analyze inconsistencies, generate question-answer pairs, and output a verdict prediction. [1] MIC (Multimodal Inconsistency Checking) focuses on whether an image’s content is consistent with the context implied by its accompanying claim, detecting contextual inconsistencies in image-claim pairs and explaining them. [4]

Some systems also argue that visual evidence should not be used indiscriminately: AMuFC adaptively uses visual evidence and reports that indiscriminate visual evidence can reduce verification accuracy. [7] Differences among the approaches include emphasis on multi-agent evidence collaboration and QA-based verdicting (VILLAIN) [1], explicit inconsistency detection with world-knowledge explanations (MIC) [4], and adaptive decision-making about whether visual evidence is necessary at all (AMuFC). [7]
